prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

Construction Spending, also referred to as Value of Construction Put in Place (VIP)

About the Survey

Purpose

To provide monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the United States (including 50 states and the District of Columbia). The population of interest includes all private residential construction and improvements, nonresidential construction, and public construction.

Coverage

Construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia).

Legal Authority and Confidentiality

Title 13, United States Code, Sections 131 and 182 authorizes the Census Bureau to conduct this collection and to request your voluntary assistance. By Section 9 of Title 13, United States Code, your report is confidential. It may be seen only by persons sworn to uphold the confidentiality of Census Bureau information, and may be used only for statistical purposes. The law also provides that copies of your report retained in your files are immune from legal process.

Primary Customers and Users

  • The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)
  • Other government agencies
  • Construction-related businesses

Products

The key statistics produced for Construction Spending are monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. The survey covers construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia). Data are shown by type of construction as seasonally adjusted annual rates and in unadjusted dollars.

Data on construction spending are available on a monthly and annual basis going back to 1993.

Statistics for construction are available at the U.S. level monthly, and by division, region, and state annually for selected categories. Private manufacturing is availalable monthly at the region and division level.

Construction spending estimates include the cost of labor and materials, architectural and engineering work, overhead, interest and taxes paid during construction, and contractor’s profits.

Construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors (in 50 states and the District of Columbia).

Value of Construction Put in Place press releases are issued on the first working day of each month, 2 months after the reference month. Data are shown by type of construction in seasonally adjusted annual rate and unadjusted dollars.

Release and Revision Schedule

Preliminary value-in-place (VIP) estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. by private or public sector and type of construction are available in the Construction Spending press release according to the release schedule.

For value-in-place estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done, two months of data are revised along with the release of each month's preliminary estimates. An analysis of the VIP revisions for estimates is updated with the release of each year's preliminary May data. With the release of preliminary May data on the Construction Spending release, seasonally adjusted annual rates for the previous 88 months are also revised to reflect updated seasonal factors. Not seasonally adjusted monthly estimates of total construction spending by owner and type of construction category are also revised to reflect late reports and revised or new estimates from outside data sources.

Beginning in 1993, the Construction Expenditures Branch of the Manufacturing and Construction Division began collecting "Value of Construction Put in Place" data for private nonresidential and state and local government projects using a new classification system. This new system allows the classification of construction with one generalized coding scheme which bases project types on their end usage instead of building/nonbuilding types. Data collection for federal construction at the detailed project level began in January 2002.

With the changes in project classifications, data now presented are not directly comparable with those data previously published in the regular-format press releases and tables. Direct comparisons can only be made at the total, total private, total state and local, total federal, and total public levels for annual and not seasonally adjusted monthly data. Although some categories (lodging, office, educational, religious) seem identical to previously published data, there have been changes within the classifications that make these values incomparable. For example, private medical office buildings were classified as "office" buildings previously, but under the new classification these buildings are in "health care."

#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Construction Spending
Description: Provides monthly estimates of the total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S. The data is collected through the Value of Construction Put in Place Survey (VIP) and covers construction work done each month on new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Construction Spending (Value of Construction Put in Place): research report

*Sources checked as of early October 2026. Most facts come from Census Bureau pages, Federal Register/OMB filings, and the Cambridge *Historical Statistics of the United States*. Where something is my inference rather than a sourced fact, I say so.*

---

## 1. Checking your description

Your title and description are accurate. They closely match the Census Bureau's own wording on the program's landing page. A few points would make them more precise:

| Your description | What I found |
|---|---|
| "Value of Construction Put in Place Survey (VIP)" | Correct. The official name is "Construction Spending, also referred to as Value of Construction Put in Place (VIP)." VIP is really a **program that combines several sources**, not one survey. Census says direct survey data make up about **65%** of the monthly total. The other **35%** is built from other Census, federal, and private sources. |
| "total dollar value of construction work done in the U.S." | Correct. Coverage is the **50 states and DC**. Puerto Rico and the territories are not included. |
| "new structures or improvements to existing structures for private and public sectors" | Correct. One nuance: residential improvements now cover **owner-occupied housing only**. Improvements to rental, vacant, and seasonal properties were dropped in 2008 after their source survey was cut for budget reasons (see §4). |
| Not mentioned | The figures are in **current dollars and are not adjusted for inflation**. The inflation-adjusted series was discontinued in 2003. This is the most common way users misread the data. |

---

## 2. Who publishes it

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau, Department of Commerce.
- **Responsible unit:** The Construction Expenditures Branch, historically part of the Manufacturing and Construction Division. It now sits in the Economic Indicators Division; the customer-service email is eid.ceb.customer.service@census.gov.
- **Status:** A **Principal Federal Economic Indicator**, one of the market-moving monthly releases. These indicators follow OMB rules on release timing and pre-release security (OMB Statistical Policy Directive No. 3, which I know from background rather than from these sources). Releases come out at **10:00 a.m. ET**.
- **Main web address:** census.gov/constructionspending (redirects to census.gov/construction/c30/). The "C30" in the URL is the old print report series, *Construction Reports C30*.

## 3. Legal authority

- **Authority to collect:** **Title 13, U.S. Code, Sections 131 and 182**. These sections authorize the collection and allow Census to request "voluntary assistance."
- **Confidentiality:** **Title 13, Section 9**. Individual responses may only be seen by sworn Census staff and used only for statistical purposes. Respondents' file copies are immune from legal process.
- **Response is voluntary.** This matters for data quality, because nonresponse has to be filled in statistically (imputed).
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** The **Construction Progress Reporting Surveys** have OMB Control No. **0607-0153**, using forms:
  - C-700: private nonresidential projects
  - C-700(R): private multifamily projects
  - C-700(SL): state and local government projects
  - C-700(F): federal projects

  The current approval (ICR 202411-0607-004) **expires August 31, 2028**. Renewal is the next formal point for public comment.
- **Respondent burden (2024 Federal Register notice):** about **22,000 respondents** and **51,333 burden hours** a year. Each response takes about 30 minutes the first month and 10 minutes after that. Projects stay in the sample about 12 months on average. BEA filed a letter supporting the collection.

## 4. History

| Period | Milestone |
|---|---|
| 1930s | The series was designed and first assembled for 1915–1937 by the Commerce Department's Division of Economic Research (Chawner, 1938). |
| 1940s–1959 | Compiled jointly by the Department of Commerce and the Department of Labor (BLS). Monthly progress was estimated "indirectly," by applying fixed construction schedules to building permits and contract awards. |
| **July 1, 1959** | **Census took over full responsibility.** |
| 1964–1975 | Direct field surveys of actual monthly progress replaced the indirect methods: single-family and nonresidential in 1964, multifamily in 1974, state and local in 1975. This created **breaks in the series in 1964**. |
| Mid-1970s | Census stopped revising pre-1964 estimates. Constant-dollar series were rebased in 1974. |
| 1993 | New classification by **end use** (e.g., "health care," "power") for private nonresidential and state/local projects. The current series starts here. |
| Jan 2002 | Detailed project-level collection of federal construction began. |
| **Aug 2003** | First release in the new format. **The old classifications and the constant (1996) dollar series were discontinued.** The old series (1964–2002) stays online as a frozen archive. |
| 2006–07 | Release date moved to the last workday of the month. It is now back to the first workday. |
| 2007 | Methodology change for state and local estimates; revised back to 1993. |
| **2008** | The Survey of Residential Alterations and Repairs was **discontinued because of budget cuts**. Improvements to rental, vacant, and seasonal properties were removed back to 1993, because no other source exists. |
| 2013, 2018–19 | Release delays during government funding lapses. |
| 2015 | Data made available through the Census economic-indicators API. |
| 2020 | COVID-19 quality notices. Multifamily imputation method revised back to 2009. |
| Feb 2023 | Launch of the **experimental Monthly Subnational Construction Spending: Private Manufacturing**, monthly estimates by Census division from 2017 on. |
| **Oct–Nov 2025** | The 43-day shutdown halted collection. August 2025 data, due Oct 1, came out **Nov 17, 2025**. |
| 2026 | Catch-up period: January 2026 data came out March 23. **February and March were combined into one May 7 release.** The normal schedule resumed June 1. |

**Long-run historical data:** Annual figures go back to **1915** in the *Historical Statistics of the United States* (Millennial Edition, Tables Dc). The editors warn about breaks at 1947 (constant dollars) and 1964. The NBER Macrohistory database holds the BLS–Commerce monthly series from 1939 to 1963.

## 5. Methodology (for data scientists)

**Sources by component:**
- **Construction Progress Reporting Surveys** (mail with online option, phone follow-up) cover private nonresidential, state/local, federal, and private multifamily.
  - Nonresidential and public projects are sampled from project lists bought from **Dodge Data & Analytics**, a commercial vendor. A small sample from areas without building permits is added.
  - The sample is stratified by owner, type, and project value.
- **New single-family:** derived from the Census **Survey of Construction** (housing starts and sales).
- **Residential improvements:** from the BLS **Consumer Expenditure Survey** (Interview component). Recent months are forecast with X-13ARIMA-SEATS, so **revisions are large**.
- **Other sources:**
  - Farm: USDA farm income and balance sheet reports, annual only
  - Railroads: Surface Transportation Board
  - Electric, gas, and oil: regulatory and industry capital spending reports
  - Cable TV: trade association statistics
  - Telephone: monthly progress reports
  - Private manufacturing: periodically benchmarked to the Annual Capital Expenditures Survey (1992, 1994, 1998, 2003, 2008, 2012, 2017)

**Estimation:** The final weight for each project is its sampling weight, adjusted for outliers, for architectural and engineering costs, and for duplicates in the sampling frame. Missing monthly values are imputed and re-imputed for up to 24 months, until the project is complete. Variance is estimated with a stratified jackknife.

**What a dollar of spending includes:** labor, materials, architectural and engineering work, overhead, interest and taxes paid during construction, and contractor profit. Land, most machinery and equipment, and maintenance and repairs are excluded.

**Release and revision cycle:**
- Data come out on the **first workday of the month, about two months after the reference month**. For example, August data come out October 1.
- Each release revises the previous two months.
- **Annual revision comes with the May data (released July 1).** Unadjusted data are revised about two years back. Seasonally adjusted data are revised five more years back (the program page cites 88 months). The 2026 revision went back to January 2024 for unadjusted data and January 2019 for adjusted data.
- Federal, utility, and railroad figures depend on outside sources that may lag a year or two.

**Uncertainty:** Releases give a ± range for each change. An asterisk means the change is not statistically significant. Many headline monthly changes fall inside that range; in August 2026, for example, total spending rose 0.9% ± 1.0%.

**Practical cautions:**
- Seasonally adjusted figures are **annual rates (SAAR)**, not monthly dollar amounts. Unadjusted figures are actual monthly dollars.
- The data are **not adjusted for inflation**. For real terms, use deflators such as BEA's structures price indexes or BLS producer price indexes (my suggestion; Census doesn't specify).
- Don't splice the pre-1993 or pre-2003 categories onto current ones. Only the top-level totals are comparable, and only for annual and unadjusted monthly data.
- **Geography is limited.** Monthly data are national only. State, region, and division data are annual and cover selected categories. Private manufacturing has monthly division data, but only as an experimental product.
- My understanding (not confirmed in this research) is that **data centers fall under the "office" category**. That would help explain the recent boom in private office spending (+29.8% year over year, August 2026).

## 6. Access and formats

- Current release as **PDF and XLSX**, plus an "at a glance" summary.
- Historical press releases in PDF and XLSX by year.
- Historical data tables, including the archived 1964–2002 old-classification tables and annual state/regional tables.
- The **Economic Indicators time-series database** ("Time Series/Trend Charts," program code VIP) and the **Census API**.
- Methodology documents, definitions, FAQs, release calendar, and the C-700 forms.
- The data are also redistributed by **FRED/ALFRED** (St. Louis Fed). ALFRED keeps past versions of each release, which is useful for studying revisions.
- Note: the program's data page currently says **"The Construction Spending visualizations will not be updated until further notice."**

## 7. Typical users

- **Bureau of Economic Analysis (the main customer):** uses it for the structures parts of GDP (residential, private nonresidential, and government investment). Construction is cited as about **7.4% of GDP**.
- **Federal Reserve Board and Treasury:** use it to forecast GDP, which feeds into monetary policy discussions.
- **Other agencies and state and local governments:** track infrastructure spending such as highways, water, sewer, and schools.
- **Construction-related businesses:** materials makers, contractors, and trade groups (for example AGC, ABC, NAHB, AIA) use it to estimate demand and plan production.
- **Financial markets, economists, and journalists:** follow it as a monthly market-moving release (Reuters, KPMG, and Haver all cover it).
- **Academic researchers:** study business cycles, housing, and the effects of industrial policy.

## 8. Public benefits

- It is the most complete measure of a major economic sector, and it feeds GDP and macroeconomic policy.
- It is free, timely, regular, and documented, with stated error ranges. That makes it a neutral reference shared by industry, government, and the public.
- It makes public investment visible. Public construction was about $548B SAAR in August 2026, including highways at about $151B and education at about $113B.
- It shows how policy plays out. For example, private manufacturing construction fell about 20% year over year as the factory-building boom of recent years wound down, while power construction rose.
- It reduces the need for private surveys and costly commercial data, which especially helps small firms and local governments.

## 9. Current status (October 2026)

- **Latest release (Oct 1, 2026, August data):** total spending was **$2,203.1B SAAR**, up 0.9% (±1.0%) from July and down 1.7% from a year earlier. Year to date was down 3.1%. Private spending was $1,655.3B and public spending $547.8B.
- **Next releases:** Nov 2, 2026 (September data); Dec 1 (October data); Jan 4, 2027 (November data).
- **Wider pressures:** The American Statistical Association reports the Census Bureau lost about 15% of its staff since FY2024, amid hiring freezes and leadership turnover. Its 2026 midyear update finds statistical agencies mostly keeping schedules but with growing strain. The FY2026 budget request held Current Economic Statistics, which includes construction, flat at $216M. I found **no announced cut to this program**, but it remains exposed to these pressures.

## 10. Notes for preservationists and data librarians

- **Risks:**
  - The survey is voluntary.
  - The sampling frame depends on a commercial vendor (Dodge).
  - A component has been cut for budget reasons before (2008).
  - Shutdowns have caused data gaps or late collection (2013, 2019, 2025).
  - Visualizations are frozen.
  - Staff losses could lead to quieter cuts in detail or experimental products.
- **Priority items to capture:**
  - All historical press releases (PDF and XLSX)
  - The 1964–2002 old-classification tables and constant-dollar deflator indexes
  - Annual state and regional tables
  - Experimental monthly subnational tables
  - Methodology PDFs, including revision analyses
  - Length-of-Time tables (released each June) and the private power table (May)
  - C-700 forms and OMB documents (ICR 0607-0153)
  - Notices on the program's "Previous Announcements" page
- **Revision history:** Monthly values change for years. Store dated versions, or use ALFRED, rather than only the latest figures.
- **Suggested catalog metadata:**
  - Creator: U.S. Census Bureau
  - Frequency: monthly, with annual tables
  - Coverage: national monthly from 1993 (current classification); 1964–2002 under the old classification; annual back to 1915 through Historical Statistics
  - Geography: U.S. (50 states and DC); state/regional annual for selected categories
  - Units: current dollars, SAAR and unadjusted
  - Rights: U.S. government work, public domain

## 11. Notes for policy advocates

- **Formal ways to weigh in:** Federal Register comment periods when the OMB approval is renewed (by 2028), Census advisory committees, and the feedback email for the experimental products.
- **Known gaps worth raising:**
  - No monthly state data
  - No inflation-adjusted series
  - No improvements to rental properties since 2008
  - Large revisions in the residential improvements component
  - Coverage excludes the territories
- **The case for funding:** The program is low-cost. Its burden is about 51,000 hours a year, but it underpins GDP, Fed analysis, and the tracking of infrastructure and industrial-policy spending. The 2008 cut is a concrete example of permanent data loss with no replacement source.

---

**Key sources:**
- Census program pages: census.gov/construction/c30/, including About, Methodology, Previous Announcements, Data, Release Schedule, and Forms
- Press releases CB25-154, CB26-75, and CB26-158
- Federal Register notices of July 16 and Nov 18, 2024 (OMB 0607-0153)
- *Historical Statistics of the United States*, Millennial Edition, Ch. Dc essay
- Reuters, Nov 14, 2025
- American Statistical Association, *The Nation's Data at Risk* (2025) and its 2026 midyear update
- CRS report IF12714 (FY2026 Census budget)

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

# Risk Assessment: Construction Spending (Value of Construction Put in Place, VIP) *Research current to October 8, 2026.* The biggest risks come from the Census Bureau as a whole: staff losses, leadership changes, and a proposed reorganization. Nothing I found targets this dataset directly. Its releases are back on schedule, its OMB approval runs to 2028, and the August 2026 data came out on time on October 1. **Corrections to my previous report:** - **Advisory committees:** I listed Census advisory committees as a way for advocates to weigh in. They no longer exist. Commerce terminated the Census Scientific Advisory Committee and the Federal Economic Statistics Advisory Committee (FESAC), along with 12 other committees, effective February 28, 2025, under Executive Order 14217 (Federal Register, June 10, 2025). - **Staffing tracker:** The USAJobs tracker you suggested stopped collecting data on December 31, 2025 and is now archived. I couldn't get current figures from it, so the staffing evidence below comes from union statements, the American Statistical Association (ASA), and news reports. --- ## 1. Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue** | Level | Evidence | |---|---| | Gone / High | None. Historical press releases (PDF and XLSX), the archived 1964–2002 tables, and the annual state/regional tables are still online. | | Moderate | The program's data page says "Construction Spending visualizations will not be updated until further notice." That freezes a viewing tool, not any data files. Separately, improvements to rental, vacant, and seasonal properties were removed back to 1993, but that happened in **2008**, long before this period. | | No Known Issue | I found no files removed and no undocumented changes since January 2025. The 2026 annual revision (unadjusted data back to January 2024, seasonally adjusted back to January 2019) is the normal, announced process. | **Why this level:** All the data is still there. The frozen visualizations are worth watching, but they aren't a loss of data. ## 2. Future Data Availability: **Moderate Risk** | Level | Evidence | |---|---| | High | Doesn't apply. The OMB approval (ICR 202411-0607-004, control no. 0607-0153) was approved August 18, 2025, before the previous approval expired on August 31, 2025. It is **active until August 31, 2028** (reginfo.gov). No release was skipped outright. | | Moderate | **Several releases came out late:**
• August 2025 data was due October 1, 2025 and came out November 17, 2025, because of the 43-day shutdown.
• January 2026 data came out March 23, 2026.
• February data (due April 1) and March data (due May 1) were **combined into one May 7, 2026 release**. Haver Analytics attributed these delays to catching up after the shutdown. | | No Known Issue | The normal schedule resumed June 1, 2026. The October 1, 2026 release was on time. The published calendar runs through December 2027. | **Why this level:** Missing scheduled dates within the past 12 months fits the "Moderate" definition. If releases stay on time through mid-2027, this could drop to No Known Issue. Future funding lapses remain the main threat. ## 3. Data Quality: **Moderate Risk** | Level | Evidence | |---|---| | High | No lasting cut to geographic or category detail, timeliness, or monthly frequency. The experimental monthly regional data for private manufacturing continues. | | Moderate | • Timeliness slipped temporarily in 2025–26, including the combined release.
• Collection paused during the shutdown, so more missing responses had to be estimated. February 2026 data came out with first-revision-quality inputs already folded in.
• Visualizations are frozen.
• The survey is voluntary, and the Bureau has lost staff Bureau-wide (see §5). | | No Known Issue | The confidence ranges in releases look normal (for example, ±0.5% on the monthly change in total spending in the January and March 2026 releases). | **Why this level:** Granularity and frequency have held up, but there are emerging risks to timeliness and capacity. ## 4. Statutory Context: **Moderate Risk** | Level | Evidence | |---|---| | High | The legal authority (13 U.S.C. §§131 and 182) lets Census run surveys in general terms. No statute names this series or requires it to be published. | | Moderate | **It isn't explicitly required by statute, but BEA relies on it to estimate the structures parts of GDP.** It is a Principal Federal Economic Indicator. The FY2026 budget materials said statistical agencies would prioritize programs that are Principal Federal Economic Indicators "or required by statute," which helps protect it. | | No Known Issue | There is no full substitute. Dodge Data & Analytics publishes private figures on project starts, but those measure contract values, not monthly work actually done, and they aren't public. Census itself buys Dodge data to build its sample. | **Why this level:** The authority is general and nothing mandates publication. That is offset by its central role in GDP and the lack of any substitute. ## 5. Staffing and Funding: **High Risk** | Level | Evidence | |---|---| | High | • **Staff lost:** about 1,300 (AP, mid-2025) to about 1,500 (Bloomberg Law, October 2025) Census employees left through deferred resignation, early retirement, or buyouts. That passes the rubric's 1,000-person threshold.
• **Layoffs:** about 100 workers at a Tucson call center received layoff notices on October 10, 2025, during the shutdown.
• **Leadership:** Director Robert Santos resigned in early 2025. The career acting director, Ron Jarmin, was replaced in September 2025 by George Cook, a political appointee at Commerce (NPR, AP). AP also reported 18 vacancies on the Bureau's leadership roster. | | Moderate | • ASA estimates the Bureau has lost about **15%** of its staff since FY2024.
• The **FY2027 budget request** cuts the Current Surveys and Programs account (where monthly economic indicators like this one are funded) from **$318.5M to $288.5M, about 9.4%**, although the Bureau's total budget would grow because of the 2030 Census (CRS R48929).
• The FY2026 request had proposed cutting that account by about 12.3%, mostly from the Survey of Income and Program Participation. | | No Known Issue | I found no reported staff or budget cuts specific to the Construction Expenditures Branch. | **Why this level:** Losing at least 1,000 staff and replacing career leadership with a political appointee both meet the "High" definition. The cuts apply to the whole Bureau; I found no figures for the branch that produces this data. ## 6. Policy: **Moderate Risk** | Level | Evidence | |---|---| | High | None found. There is no presidentially driven change to the survey's OMB approval and no negative notice on the program site. | | Moderate | **Changes that have been proposed or are pending:**
• The FY2026 and FY2027 budgets propose combining BLS, BEA, and Census under Commerce's Under Secretary for Economic Affairs, and moving BLS into Commerce.
• The FY2026 budget justification commits to eliminating functions "not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" by the end of FY2026.
• The FY2027 justification describes a shift from a "survey-centric" to a "data-centric" model that leans more on administrative and other data sources.
• Advisory committees, including FESAC, were terminated in 2025. | | No Known Issue / neutral | A Federal Register notice published October 2, 2026 (document 2026-20249) lets BEA use company-level responses from several Census surveys, including the **Construction Progress Reporting Surveys**, the main surveys behind this dataset. The notice says this is meant to improve accuracy and reduce duplicate surveys, which suggests the data is still valued. | **Why this level:** No action has targeted the dataset, but large reorganizations and plans to cut "non-core" functions are pending. Its status as a Principal Federal Economic Indicator offers some protection. --- ## Summary of risk levels - **Historical Data Availability:** No Known Issue - **Future Data Availability:** Moderate Risk - **Data Quality:** Moderate Risk - **Statutory Context:** Moderate Risk - **Staffing and Funding:** High Risk - **Policy:** Moderate Risk **Key sources:** - Census release schedule and the January and March 2026 press releases - reginfo.gov, ICR 202411-0607-004 - Federal Register: 2025-10398 (June 10, 2025) and 2026-20249 (October 2, 2026) - CRS R48929 (FY2027 appropriations for Commerce, Justice, Science) - The Census Project's summaries of the FY2026 and FY2027 budget justifications - ASA, *The Nation's Data at Risk* (Census chapter) - AP, NPR, Bloomberg Law, and Government Executive reporting on staffing and leadership - Haver Analytics on the post-shutdown catch-up releases
